title: Testing push and pull designs

accuracy.evidence: Checked on 26 Nov 2026 against NGSS K-PS2-2 ('Analyze data to determine if a design solution works as intended to change the speed or direction of an object with a push or a pull'; clarification statement examples: a ramp to increase the speed of a ball, a structure that would cause an object such as a marble or ball to turn; assessment boundary: no friction as a mechanism) and its K-PS2.B and ETS1.A disciplinary core ideas (pushes and pulls can change speed or direction; a situation people want to change can be approached as a problem solved through engineering). The physics stays inside that boundary: a bigger push makes the ball go further, a push along the line of motion changes only its speed, and a slanted wall pushes it a new way. The wall is drawn as '/' so a ball rolling right bounces up (angle in equals angle out), corrected after a screenshot showed it slanted the wrong way. Tally facts were checked: 4 of 5, 2 of 5 and every numeric item at its range corners.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented slips for young designers and forces: 'the hardest push is best' (step 1 prediction, the 'hard' slip; the hard push rolls past the mat); deciding from one trial (step 2 prediction 'one try shows it works', disproved when test 3 stops short on a bump; the 'once' slip; NGSS K-2 ETS1 and Year 1-2 working scientifically stress repeated observation); believing a stronger push can make a ball turn (step 3 prediction and 'Push harder' tile that only goes straight; the 'turn' slip); changing the goal instead of the design (step 5 'Move the mat closer' and 'Move the goal' options; the 'goal' slip); and judging by the last trial rather than the whole tally (step 4 question 3 and the 'count' slip).

lab_distinct.evidence: The mechanism is the K-PS2-2 test-and-judge cycle with pushes: three pushes with a recorded result each, a five-trial tally of one push followed by a verdict, a drag-a-wall deflection task seen from above with three spots and a goal, a two-design tick chart to read, and failed tests to fix by changing the design. It is not flagramp (steeper slopes make cars go further), flagshove (sorting pushes and pulls), flagdesign (loading foil boats until they sink) or flagswing (pendulum timing); the turning task and the data verdicts are specific to judging whether a push design changes speed or direction as intended.

lab_teaches.evidence: Children find the right push by trying all three and seeing the ball stop short, on the mat or past it; they discover that one success is not proof when test 3 misses, and then judge from 4 ticks out of 5; they find that only a wall in the right spot turns the ball (wrong spots turn it too soon or too late, a harder push goes straight); then they apply the rule by fixing three failed tests. Each done message names what they found, and the kid text confirms it afterwards.

predictions.evidence: Three predictions, each with a tempting wrong option the lab disproves: 'the hardest push' (it rolls past the mat), 'No: one try shows it works' (test 3 stops short on a bump), and 'A harder push' to make it turn (the Push harder tile sends the ball straight past the goal). The reveal line names the child's prediction once the task is done.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six rotating challenge questions; each wrong option carries a slip tag with its own message: 'hard' (harder is not always better, too hard rolls past), 'once' (one try can be lucky, test again and count), 'turn' (a push along the same line only changes speed; a wall pushes it a new way), 'goal' (keep the goal, change the design) and 'count' (count all the ticks, not one try). Lab steps give item-specific replies too, e.g. 'The wall at A turned the ball, but too soon. It missed the goal.'

readability.evidence: validate_lessons.py passes the kid (6.5) and adult (9.5) limits; the kid text scores below grade 1 (short sentences, everyday words: push, test, tick, cross, wall, mat). Lab instructions are one short line each, pictures carry the scene (ball, mat, star, goal, hand, wall) and the fig has the young class, so buttons are at least 56 px.

no_filler.evidence: Every sentence either teaches a part of testing a push design (the job, the push size, repeat trials, ticks and crosses, turning with a wall, fixing the design not the goal) or checks it. The content gate found no filler phrases and the explanation is under the 12% similarity limit against every other lesson.

mobile.evidence: Screenshots at iPhone 13 (390 px) in light and dark themes and on desktop for every step before and after Show me: the lane, the three push tiles, the tally boxes and Test tile, the top-down floor with spots A, B and C, the two ramp charts and the fix tiles all fit. The ramp chart's '2 of 5' label overlapped the last tick at 390 px, so the ticks were made smaller on narrow screens. A real pointer drag of the wall onto A (wrong) and B (right) on iPhone 13 gave 'The wall at A turned the ball, but too soon' and 'In! The wall turned the ball up into the goal.'

accessibility.evidence: Every canvas action has a button twin with a descriptive aria-label ('Roll the ball with a hard push', 'Run test 3 of 5 with the medium push', 'Put the wall at spot B and roll the ball', 'Push the ball harder with no wall', 'Fix: A bigger push'), so dragging and tapping the canvas are optional. The canvas aria-label updates with every result, the challenge feedback is a polite live region, and the browser gate ran axe WCAG 2.1 AA in both themes on desktop and iPhone 13 with no violations or console errors. Ticks and crosses are always paired with words ('on the mat', 'stopped short') so colour is never the only cue.

sources: NGSS Lead States (2013) Next Generation Science Standards, K-PS2-2 Motion and Stability: Forces and Interactions, with clarification statement and assessment boundary; K-2-ETS1-1 and K-2-ETS1-3 Engineering Design
DfE (2013) National Curriculum in England: science programmes of study, Key Stage 1 Working scientifically ('performing simple tests', 'gathering and recording data to help in answering questions')
NSTA / NGSS Appendix I: Engineering design in the NGSS (define, develop, optimise; test and compare solutions)
